blocks.prompt: The Tiny Thing Everything Is Made Of
blocks.text: Look at your hand. It looks solid. But it is built from tiny pieces called atoms. Atoms are so small that you cannot see one, not even with a school microscope. Millions and millions of them fit on the tip of your pencil. Atoms come in different kinds. One kind is called oxygen. You breathe it in. One kind is called iron. It makes nails hard and strong. One kind is called gold. It is shiny and yellow. Every kind of atom is a different building block. Put them together in new ways and you get new things. A rock. A leaf. A tooth. You.

blocks.prompt: The Marble That Is Mostly Nothing
blocks.text: Hold a marble in your hand. It feels solid and full. It is not. If you could zoom in, past the point where your eyes give up, you would find that the marble is built from atoms, and that each atom is almost entirely empty. At the middle of an atom sits a tiny clump called the nucleus. It holds protons, and usually neutrons packed in beside them. Far outside the nucleus, electrons move in a fast blur. Here is the strange part. The nucleus is thousands of times smaller than the whole atom. Imagine an atom blown up to the size of a sports stadium. The nucleus would be a pea sitting on the center spot. Everything else is empty. So why does the marble feel solid? Because the electrons on the outside of one atom push away the electrons on the outside of the next atom. You never really touch anything. You feel the push. The word atom comes from an old Greek word meaning uncuttable. People once believed you could never split one. They were wrong, but the name stuck.

blocks.prompt: Everything, From One Number
blocks.text: Every atom is built the same way, out of the same three parts, and yet atoms make everything from air to bone to gold. The trick is in the counting. At the center of an atom is the nucleus, a dense knot of protons and neutrons. Protons carry a positive electric charge. Neutrons carry none. Around the nucleus, electrons move in a blur, each carrying a negative charge. The positive nucleus pulls on the negative electrons, and that pull is what holds the atom together. What makes one atom different from another is simply the number of protons in its nucleus. One proton, and you have hydrogen, the lightest thing there is. Six protons, and you have carbon, the backbone of every living thing. Eight, oxygen. Seventy-nine, gold. Change the proton count and you change the substance entirely. Nothing else about the recipe matters as much. For a long time nobody knew the nucleus was there. In 1909, working in Ernest Rutherford's laboratory, two scientists fired tiny particles at a sheet of gold foil so thin it was nearly transparent. Almost every particle sailed straight through, exactly as expected. But a few came bouncing back. Rutherford was astonished. Something small, hard, and heavy had to be hiding inside each atom, and almost everything else had to be empty space. That was the nucleus. The scale still stops people. If an atom were enlarged to the size of a cathedral, the nucleus would be a pinhead hanging in the middle of it. The rest is the electrons and their emptiness. When you knock on a table, you are not touching wood. You are feeling the electrons in your knuckles push back against the electrons in the table, across a gap they never close.

blocks.prompt: The Uncuttable Thing That Got Cut
blocks.text: For most of human history, the atom was an argument rather than an object. Around 2,400 years ago a Greek thinker named Democritus reasoned that if you kept cutting a piece of cheese in half, you would eventually reach a piece that could not be cut again. He called it atomos, the uncuttable. He had no evidence. It was a guess, and it sat unproven for more than two thousand years. The evidence arrived in pieces, and each piece embarrassed the one before it. In 1803 John Dalton showed that chemicals always combine in fixed, tidy ratios, which makes sense only if matter comes in indivisible units. In 1897 J. J. Thomson found something smaller than an atom: a light, negatively charged particle we now call the electron. The uncuttable had been cut. In 1909, in Ernest Rutherford's laboratory, researchers fired particles at gold foil and watched a few of them ricochet straight back, which meant the atom's mass was crammed into a minuscule core. In 1932 James Chadwick identified the neutron sharing that core with the protons. The picture that emerged is stranger than a solid ball. An atom is a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons, and the nucleus is roughly one hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself. Almost the entire volume is empty. Worse for our intuitions, the electrons do not circle the nucleus like planets. Since Erwin Schrodinger's work in 1926, physicists describe them as clouds of probability: an electron has no definite path, only a region where it is likely to be found. Yet the emptiness is not weakness. Those electron clouds repel each other so fiercely that they hold up buildings, bones, and bridges. When your hand rests on a desk, no part of you contacts any part of the wood. Electrons push against electrons across a gap that never closes. One last fact rearranges the rest. Nearly every atom in your body was manufactured somewhere else. Hydrogen was forged minutes after the Big Bang. The carbon in your muscles and the oxygen in your blood were fused inside stars that died before the Sun existed. The atoms are not new. You are a temporary arrangement of very old parts.

blocks.prompt: Named After a Mistake: The Atom's Long Argument
blocks.text: The atom is named after a mistake. Around 400 BC, the Greek philosopher Democritus argued that matter could not be divided forever. Keep halving a lump of gold, he said, and you must eventually arrive at a particle that resists any further cut. He named it atomos, meaning uncuttable. Democritus had no instrument, no experiment, and no evidence. He had an argument. It was correct in spirit and wrong in the one detail his name preserved, because the atom can be cut, and the twentieth century spent much of its energy cutting it. The proof took 2,200 years to arrive, and it arrived in installments. In 1803 John Dalton noticed that elements combine in small whole-number ratios, never in messy fractions, a pattern that makes sense only if matter is grainy rather than smooth. In 1897 J. J. Thomson, studying rays in a vacuum tube, found a particle almost two thousand times lighter than the lightest atom. He had discovered the electron, and with it the uncomfortable fact that the uncuttable had parts. In 1909, in Ernest Rutherford's laboratory in Manchester, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden aimed a beam of alpha particles at a sheet of gold foil. The expectation was that everything would pass through with a slight deflection. Almost everything did. But roughly one particle in eight thousand rebounded backward, as though it had struck something immovable. Rutherford concluded that an atom's mass and positive charge are concentrated in a nucleus so small that the rest of the atom is essentially vacant. In 1932 James Chadwick found the neutron alongside the proton in that nucleus, and the modern picture was complete. Complete, but not intuitive. The nucleus is about one hundred thousand times smaller than the atom that contains it. Enlarge an atom to the length of a football field and the nucleus is a grain of sand on the center line. The identity of the atom, meanwhile, is set by one number: the count of protons in that grain. One proton is hydrogen. Six is carbon. Eight is oxygen. Seventy-nine is gold. Add a proton and the substance becomes something else entirely, with different color, different weight, and different behavior. Everything you have ever touched is a rearrangement of that single variable. And the electrons are stranger than the textbook diagram admits. They are usually drawn as tiny balls looping around the nucleus, which is a useful lie. Erwin Schrodinger's mathematics, published in 1926, describes them instead as standing clouds of probability. An electron does not have a path. It has a region where it is likely to be found, and asking where it is between measurements is closer to a category error than to a question. This is where the familiar phrase mostly empty space begins to mislead. Nothing about an atom feels empty from the outside. Those probability clouds resist compression so violently that they support skyscrapers and stop your hand at the surface of a desk. You have never touched anything in your life. You have felt electrons refusing electrons across a gap they never bridge, and your brain reports it as solidity. There is one more inversion. The atoms in your body are not yours and are not new. Hydrogen condensed out of the cooling universe about 13.8 billion years ago. The carbon in your cells and the oxygen in your lungs were fused in the cores of stars that lived and exploded before the Sun ignited. Iron in your blood was welded together in exploding stars, and the gold in a wedding ring may trace back to a collision between two dead stars. Democritus was searching for the smallest possible thing. He found, without knowing it, the oldest thing you will ever hold.
